note: Marketing lesson, content v3 (28 words, 1 grammar rule). Course level B1.1 (Gateway level 9), unit Marketing, from the Anki Marketing export.

words.meaning: A planned series of activities, like ads and posts, to reach one business goal.
situations: The shop ran a two-month campaign with TV ads, posters and online videos to sell its new juice.
gaps: Our summer ______ on Instagram brought in 3,000 new followers.
The company spent a lot of money on an advertising ______ for its new phone.
hints: A planned group of ads or actions with one goal.

commonMistakes.sentence: They started a new campain on TV.
commonMistakes.correction: They started a new campaign on TV.
commonMistakes.why: The spelling has a silent 'g': campaign.

words.meaning: Using new and original ideas or ways of doing things.
situations: Instead of normal ads, the brand hid prizes inside a phone game — nobody had done that before.
gaps: The company is famous for its ______ products — it's always the first to try new ideas.
We need an ______ idea, not the same old poster.
hints: Describes something new, original and creative.

commonMistakes.sentence: Their design is very innovation.
commonMistakes.correction: Their design is very innovative.
commonMistakes.why: 'Innovation' is a noun; use the adjective 'innovative' after 'very'.

words.meaning: The moral rules about what is right and wrong in how people or companies behave.
situations: The company refused to use child workers, even though it would have been cheaper.
gaps: Lying to customers in ads goes against good business ______.
Many young people only buy from brands with strong ______.
hints: Moral principles about right and wrong.

commonMistakes.sentence: He has no ethic at work.
commonMistakes.correction: He has no ethics at work.
commonMistakes.why: 'Ethics' (moral principles) is normally used in the plural form.

words.meaning: An advertisement on TV or radio; also, connected with buying and selling for profit.
situations: During the football match, a 30-second ad for a new car came on between the two halves.
gaps: I hate it when a movie stops for a long ______ break.
The film was a big ______ success — it made millions.
hints: A TV or radio ad — or anything about making money from selling.

commonMistakes.sentence: I saw a funny commercial in the newspaper.
commonMistakes.correction: I saw a funny advert in the newspaper.
commonMistakes.why: A 'commercial' is on TV or radio; in print it's an ad or advert.

words.meaning: A firm promise that something will happen or that a product will work, or you get your money back.
situations: The shop promised: 'If you don't like it in 30 days, we'll give you all your money back.'
gaps: They offer a money-back ______ if you're not happy.
I can't ______ that the package will arrive tomorrow.
hints: A promise — often 'money-back'. Also a verb: to promise something will happen.

commonMistakes.sentence: I guarantee you that you will like it to.
commonMistakes.correction: I guarantee that you will like it.
commonMistakes.why: Use 'guarantee (that) + clause' — keep it simple.

words.meaning: Controlling or influencing people in a clever, unfair way to get what you want.
situations: The ad showed sad children to make viewers feel guilty so they would buy the toy — that's playing with feelings unfairly.
gaps: Using fear to sell a product is a kind of emotional ______.
The report showed clear ______ of the sales numbers.
hints: The noun: the act of controlling people unfairly.

commonMistakes.sentence: He is good at manipulation people.
commonMistakes.correction: He is good at manipulating people.
commonMistakes.why: 'Manipulation' is a noun; after 'at' use the verb + -ing: manipulating.

words.meaning: Selling goods directly to the public, usually in shops or online.
situations: She works in a clothes shop at the mall, helping people choose and pay for jeans.
gaps: She has worked in ______ for years — first in a bookshop, now in a phone store.
The ______ price of this TV is $500, but online it's cheaper.
hints: Selling to ordinary customers in shops — the opposite of selling in bulk.

commonMistakes.sentence: He works in retailer.
commonMistakes.correction: He works in retail.
commonMistakes.why: 'Retail' is the business; a 'retailer' is the shop or company.

words.meaning: Good enough to compete with others, especially with low prices — or wanting very much to win.
situations: Their prices are a bit lower than every other shop in town, so people choose them.
gaps: The shop offers very ______ prices, so it's always busy.
My brother is so ______ — he gets angry if he loses a game.
hints: Describes prices that can beat rivals, or a person who hates to lose.

commonMistakes.sentence: They have very competitor prices.
commonMistakes.correction: They have very competitive prices.
commonMistakes.why: 'Competitor' is a person or company; use the adjective 'competitive'.

words.meaning: A person whose job is to arrange and show products in shops so customers notice and buy them.
situations: Every Monday, Omar moves the new chocolates to the shelf at eye level near the checkout.
gaps: The ______ put the summer clothes in the shop window to attract shoppers.
As a ______, she decides how products look on the shelves.
hints: The person who displays products in shops.

commonMistakes.sentence: He works as a merchandise in the supermarket.
commonMistakes.correction: He works as a merchandiser in the supermarket.
commonMistakes.why: 'Merchandise' is the goods; the person is a 'merchandiser'.

words.meaning: Possible in the future but not real yet; or the ability to develop and succeed later.
situations: People who visited the website but haven't bought anything yet could become buyers one day.
gaps: We sent free samples to 500 ______ customers.
This small café has the ______ to become a big chain.
hints: Possible, not real yet — like a future customer.

commonMistakes.sentence: She has a lot of potentials.
commonMistakes.correction: She has a lot of potential.
commonMistakes.why: As 'ability to succeed', 'potential' is uncountable — no 's'.

words.meaning: To control or influence someone in a clever, unfair way to get what you want.
situations: The salesman said 'only one left!' even though the store room was full, just to make me buy quickly.
gaps: Some ads ______ children into wanting expensive toys.
Don't let him ______ you — think for yourself.
hints: The verb: to control people unfairly.

commonMistakes.sentence: He manipulated me to buy it.
commonMistakes.correction: He manipulated me into buying it.
commonMistakes.why: Use 'manipulate someone into doing something'.

words.meaning: Good for you, healthy, and morally good — nothing harmful.
situations: The ad showed a happy family eating fresh vegetables together at a farm table.
gaps: The cereal has a ______ image — natural, healthy and family-friendly.
It's a ______ family film with no bad language.

commonMistakes.sentence: They sell wholesome to supermarkets.
commonMistakes.correction: They sell wholesale to supermarkets.
commonMistakes.why: 'Wholesome' means healthy and good; selling in bulk is 'wholesale'.

words.meaning: A person or company that buys goods in large amounts and sells them to shops, not to the public.
situations: The company buys 10,000 bottles of water from the factory and sells them in boxes to small shops.
gaps: The supermarket gets its rice from a ______ at a low price.
You can't buy just one T-shirt from a ______ — they sell in big boxes to shops.
hints: The company in the middle: factory → ___ → shop.

commonMistakes.sentence: I bought one shirt from the wholesaler.
commonMistakes.correction: I bought one shirt from the shop.
commonMistakes.why: Wholesalers sell large amounts to shops, not single items to the public.

words.meaning: A person or company that tries to win customers from others selling the same thing.
situations: Pepsi and Coca-Cola both try to win the same customers in every country.
gaps: Before setting our prices, we checked what our main ______ charges.
She is our biggest ______ — she sells the same cakes on the same street.

commonMistakes.sentence: They are our biggest competition company.
commonMistakes.correction: They are our biggest competitor.
commonMistakes.why: Use the noun 'competitor' for the rival company.

words.meaning: A written document from the maker saying they will repair or replace a product if it breaks within a set time.
situations: My laptop screen broke after eight months, so the company fixed it for free — it was still covered.
gaps: The washing machine is still under ______, so they'll repair it for free.
This phone comes with a one-year ______.

commonMistakes.sentence: My phone is under guarantee for repair paper.
commonMistakes.correction: My phone is under warranty.
commonMistakes.why: A 'warranty' is the written repair promise; say 'under warranty'.

words.meaning: A person who buys goods or services from a shop or business.
situations: A woman walks into the bakery, buys two loaves of bread, pays and leaves.
gaps: The shop gave every ______ a free coffee on opening day.
The ______ wanted to return the shoes because they were too small.
hints: Someone who buys things in a shop.

commonMistakes.sentence: The lawyer has many customers.
commonMistakes.correction: The lawyer has many clients.
commonMistakes.why: Professionals like lawyers have 'clients'; shops have 'customers'.

words.meaning: A person or company that pays a professional, like a lawyer or an agency, for a service.
situations: The ad agency meets the hotel owner every month to plan his next advertising project.
gaps: The lawyer met her ______ to talk about the case.
Our agency's biggest ______ is a famous sports brand.
hints: Someone who pays a professional for a service, not a shop.

commonMistakes.sentence: The supermarket has many clients.
commonMistakes.correction: The supermarket has many customers.
commonMistakes.why: Shops have 'customers'; professionals and agencies have 'clients'.

words.meaning: To make someone believe that something is true.
situations: At first I thought the cream was a scam, but after seeing the real test results I believed it worked.
gaps: The test results finally ______d me that the product was safe.
She tried to ______ her boss that the idea was good.
hints: Change what someone believes is true.

commonMistakes.sentence: He convinced me buying the car.
commonMistakes.correction: He persuaded me to buy the car.
commonMistakes.why: 'Convince' is mainly about belief (convince someone that…); for getting someone to act, 'persuade someone to do' is more natural.

words.meaning: To make someone do something by giving them good reasons.
situations: My friend didn't want to join the gym, but I talked to her for an hour and she signed up the next day.
gaps: The salesman ______d me to buy the bigger TV.
Can you ______ your dad to lend us the car?
hints: Get someone to do something with good reasons.

commonMistakes.sentence: She persuaded me buying it.
commonMistakes.correction: She persuaded me to buy it.
commonMistakes.why: Use 'persuade someone to do something'.

words.meaning: When a baby bird comes out of its egg; also, to secretly plan something.
situations: After three weeks, the eggs cracked open and small yellow chicks came out.
gaps: The chicks will ______ next week.
The two friends ______ed a plan to start their own business.
hints: What eggs do when babies come out.

commonMistakes.sentence: The egg hatched a chick out.
commonMistakes.correction: The chick hatched.
commonMistakes.why: Say 'the egg hatched' or 'the chick hatched' — no 'out'.

words.meaning: To secretly tell someone in charge that another person did something wrong (informal).
situations: When Ali took money from the till, his co-worker went straight to the manager and told her.
gaps: Don't ______ on me to the teacher!
Nobody trusts him at work because he's a ______.
hints: To tell on someone — informal and negative.

commonMistakes.sentence: He snitched me to the boss.
commonMistakes.correction: He snitched on me to the boss.
commonMistakes.why: Use 'snitch on someone'.

words.meaning: Selling goods in large amounts at low prices to shops, not to the public.
situations: The café owner buys coffee beans in 50-kilo bags at a low price, then sells cups of coffee to people.
gaps: We buy our flour ______ because it's much cheaper in big bags.
The ______ price is much lower than the price in shops.
hints: Buying or selling in bulk to shops.

commonMistakes.sentence: He buys wholesome and sells retail.
commonMistakes.correction: He buys wholesale and sells retail.
commonMistakes.why: Bulk selling is 'wholesale'; 'wholesome' means healthy.

words.meaning: Good at making people believe or do something.
situations: Her speech was so strong that the whole team agreed to her plan in five minutes.
gaps: The ad was so ______ that I bought the product the same day.
He's a very ______ speaker — people always agree with him.
hints: Describes an argument or person that makes you agree.

commonMistakes.sentence: Her argument was very persuading.
commonMistakes.correction: Her argument was very persuasive.
commonMistakes.why: The adjective is 'persuasive'.

words.meaning: Easy to remember and pleasant, so it stays in your head.
situations: I heard the burger ad song once on the radio, and I was singing it all day.
gaps: Their slogan is so ______ — everyone at school repeats it.
The song has a ______ tune that you can't forget.
hints: Describes a song or slogan that sticks in your head.

commonMistakes.sentence: That's a catching slogan.
commonMistakes.correction: That's a catchy slogan.
commonMistakes.why: The adjective is 'catchy', not 'catching'.

words.word: Don't count your chickens before they hatch
words.meaning: Don't make plans based on something good before it has actually happened.
situations: Sami started spending his bonus money before his boss had even agreed to give it to him.
gaps: You haven't got the job yet — ______!
I know the client seems happy, but ______. The contract isn't signed.
hints: Wait until good results really happen before celebrating.
An idiom about chickens and eggs.

commonMistakes.sentence: Don't count your eggs before they hatch.
commonMistakes.correction: Don't count your chickens before they hatch.
commonMistakes.why: The fixed idiom uses 'chickens'.

words.meaning: Something that will cause either great success or total failure.
situations: If the new restaurant doesn't get customers this month, it will have to close for good.
gaps: This meeting is ______ for our company — if they say no, we close.
The first week of sales will ______ the new product.
hints: Two opposite verbs joined by 'or' — total success or total failure.

commonMistakes.sentence: It's a break or make moment.
commonMistakes.correction: It's a make-or-break moment.
commonMistakes.why: The fixed order is 'make or break'.

words.meaning: To be tricked into believing something that is not true.
situations: The photo showed a big pizza, but the real one was tiny — and I still paid for it.
gaps: I can't believe I ______ that fake ad!
Don't ______ his lies — he says that to everyone.

commonMistakes.sentence: I fell to the trick.
commonMistakes.correction: I fell for the trick.
commonMistakes.why: The phrasal verb is 'fall for'.

words.meaning: Old-fashioned, too obvious, or trying too hard to be funny or cool (informal).
situations: My dad told the same old 'why did the chicken cross the road' joke at dinner, and everyone groaned.
gaps: That joke was so ______ — nobody laughed.
The ad used a ______ slogan that sounded like the 1980s.
hints: A joke or line that is too old or obvious — like 'basic'.

commonMistakes.sentence: The joke was very corn.
commonMistakes.correction: The joke was very corny.
commonMistakes.why: The adjective is 'corny'.

grammar.rule: Was / were supposed to: a past plan or expectation
grammar.explanation: Use was/were supposed to + base verb for something that was planned or expected but did NOT happen. Present: am/is/are (not) supposed to = what you should or shouldn't do.
examples: I was supposed to attend the meeting, but I was sick.
You aren't supposed to be here.
They were supposed to launch the ad last week.

commonMistakes.sentence: I was suppose to call you.
commonMistakes.correction: I was supposed to call you.
commonMistakes.why: Always 'supposed' with -d.

commonMistakes.sentence: We were supposed to finished it.
commonMistakes.correction: We were supposed to finish it.
commonMistakes.why: After 'supposed to', use the base verb.

questions.prompt: The campaign ______ start on Monday, but the posters weren't ready.
questions.explanation: was/were + supposed to + base verb for a plan that didn't happen.

questions.prompt: Which sentence means the plan did NOT happen?
options: I was supposed to email the client yesterday.
I email the client every day.
questions.answer: I was supposed to email the client yesterday.
questions.explanation: 'Was supposed to' shows an expectation that didn't happen.

questions.sentence: They were supposed to sending the samples last week.
questions.fix: They were supposed to send the samples last week.
questions.explanation: After 'supposed to', use the base verb: send.

questions.sentence: You aren't supposed to park here.
questions.explanation: Present 'aren't supposed to' = you shouldn't do it.
questions.alternative: You aren't suppose to park here.

questions.sentence: She was suppose to call the customer.
questions.answer: She was supposed to call the customer.
